narrative:
The model determined that you have an 83% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. By far the strongest influence was your LSAT score of 24. This is substantially below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, and it pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year and third-year school decile rankings were the next two most important factors. Both were also below the averages of accepted students (5 versus 6 in year one, and 4 versus 5.8 in year three), each adding a moderate push toward a higher risk of failing the bar.

Taken together, these academic performance signals led the model to conclude that the likelihood of passing the bar on the first try was too low for admission.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a significantly higher score, while also improving your law school grades to reach higher deciles, would be the most effective steps. Once those numbers rise, reapplying would give the model a very different picture of your likelihood of success.
